# Project Aim 
The aim of this project is to examine which aspects of early education the
school should prioritise to maximise pupils’ development during the kindergarten
years and their success throughout the rest of their school career. 
Specifically, two sub-questions which could be explored are: 

1. *What effects does spending a longer period in kindergarten have on pupils’*
*cognitive, social-emotional and executive development, and on their*
*functioning in Years 3 and 4?*  

In order to examine this question the data will need to contain information 
pertaining to (a) the amount of years/months children spent in kindergarten,
(b) enough variation in terms of how long they spent in kindergarten, to enable
a comparison between children who stayed longer, (c) variables that provide
information about their cognitive, social-emotional and executive development
and lastly (d) information about these pupils that are now in grade 3 or above. 

2. *What effects does a teaching focus on learning objectives aligned with*
*Years 3 and 4 have on pupils’ academic achievement and subsequent educational* 
*pathways?*  
Will need to be examined in a similar manner. 


# Importing Data 
Running the code below and loading the data should work if you create a 
folder named "data" in our repository and copy all the data files into this folder.
This folder is in .gitignore so will not be uploaded online but will stay in 
your local environment. 


## 1. Pupils 
The pupil data is such that each variable is of the correct type and column 
names do not contain any spaces. 
- imported such that the dates are of type date. These are now
in the format YYYY-mm-dd. The column names have been changed to contain no 
spaces. old_name = "new_name"  

- Pupil ID = "ID"
- Date of birth	= "birth_date" 
- Current class	= "curr_class"
- Current year group = 	"curr_year_group" 
- Pupil	= "pupil" 
- Start date = "start_date"

```{r importing pupil data}
# import the pupil data set with the correct data types 
pupils <- read_xlsx(here::here("data", "Pupils.xlsx"),
                    col_names = c("ID", "birth_date", "curr_class",
                                  "curr_year_group", "pupil", "start_date"),
                    skip = 1, # drops the original header row 
                    col_types = c("text", "date", "text",
                                  "text", "text", "date")) |>
  mutate(birth_date = as.Date(birth_date),
         curr_year_group = as.numeric(curr_year_group),
         start_date = as.Date(start_date)) 
        

pupils
```


### Pupil Selection 
Firstly, the pupile data provides information about the current group of the
pupils. As we need information about how these pupils performed in group 3-4,
pupils currently in the startergroup,  group 1, and group 2, cannot be included
in our analysis. Therefore, pupils currently in group 0, 1, and 2 will be 
filtered out. After removing these pupils the data set contains 104 entries. 
The names of these 104 pupils are stored in a vector which will be employed to 
extract their data from other files. 


```{r pupil selection}
# filter out pupils currently in the startgroup, group 1 or group 2 
pupil_selection <- pupils |>
  filter(curr_year_group %in% 3:7)

pupil_selection
```

```{r store pupil names}
# store the names of all the pupils currently in grade 3-7 
pupil_names <- pupil_selection |> pull(pupil)

pupil_names
```

## 2. Observations group 1 and 2 
This data file contains observations from students in group 1 and 2. Firstly, 
the data is imported in the correct format. Secondly, only the rows containing 
information of the selected pupils above is retained. After filtering the data, 
this file contains 96821 rows. 
```{r importing observation year 1/2 data}
observations_1_2 <- read_xlsx(here::here("data", "Observaties_groep_1_2.xlsx"),
                              sheet = 1, # select only first tab in excel file 
                              col_types = c("skip", "text", "text", "text",
                                            "text", "text", "text", "date",
                                            "numeric", "text", "text", "text")) |>
  mutate(Score = as.numeric(Score), Datum = as.Date(Datum)) # convert type 
```


```{r filter selected pupils}
# only keep data about the pupils as selected above 
observation_selection <-
  observations_1_2 |>
  filter(Leerling %in% pupil_names)

observation_selection
```


# Time spent in Kindergarten 
In order to examine how long each pupil stayed in kindergarten, and whether 
these periods differ enough between pupils to compare between groups, we will 
need to determine how long each pupil spent in kindergarten.  

This could be estimated from the start date of each pupil and the last observation
which was made for them in group 1/2. This will not provide a precise estimate
but will give us a rough estimation of whether we can proceed. 
```{r kindergarden time compution}
# store the date of the first, last and number of observations for each pupil 
last_observation <- observation_selection |>
  group_by(Leerling) |>
  summarise(first_obs = min(Datum, na.rm = TRUE),
            last_obs  = max(Datum, na.rm = TRUE),
            n_obs     = n()) # can check how complete the pupils record is 

# join the days spent in kindergarten to the pupil data 
kindergarten_time <- pupil_selection |>
  left_join(last_observation,
            by = c("pupil" = "Leerling")) |>
  # kindergarten days = last observation - start school 
  mutate(kindergarten_days  = as.numeric(last_obs - start_date),
         kindergarten_years = kindergarten_days / 365) 

kindergarten_time
```
## Robustness Checks 
Eyebaling the days spent in kindergarten above indicate there are differences
in time spent in kindergarten. However, a few assumptions have been made which 
need to be verified to ensure this is truly representative of their time spent
in kindergarten.  

Firstly, the variable start_date has now been interperted as 
the date at which pupils start school. The following checks will therefore be 
performed, by computing the number of days between the childs 4th birthday 
and the start date at school. (a) whether the start_date is after the child's 
4th birthday (flag potential mistakes in the data), (b) the child started school
no more than 60 days after their birthday (as this school only accepts children
that just turned 4), (c) there are no observations before the start date.  

Secondly, the time spent in kindergarten has now been estimated from the date 
at which the last observation was made in grade 1/2 of each pupil. However,
if these dates differ significanlty or were registered a long time before the 
summer holiday (July/ August) we cannot infer how long these children spent in 
kindergarten. Therefore, the second checks verifies whether the last observation 
was in july or august (and is not missing).  

Thirdly, as a robustness check we can verify whether the pupils current grade year 
corresponds to the year which they left kindergarten. First by looking at which
year the pupil left kindergarten. As school year run from September to August,
if the last observation was made between January and August the pupil left 
kindergarten that year, otherwise the year after. If this calculation is correct,
then the expected_end_year should be equal to the end year. Sp for pupils now 
in grade 4, the end of kindergarten should have been in 2025, and pupils in group 3
2026. e.g. reference year = 2026, current group year = 4 -3 = 1, so ended kindergarten 
in 2025.  

To analyse which pupils fail these checks and why, a table is shown below with 
which pupils failed which check together with the information which could explain
why these checks failed. 

```{r}
ref_year <- 2026   # start year of the school year the "current group" refers to

kindergarten_checked <- kindergarten_time |>
  mutate(
    # CHECK 1: start date correct
    days_after_4th_bday = as.numeric(start_date - (birth_date %m+% years(4))),
    check_start = days_after_4th_bday >= 0 &
                  days_after_4th_bday <= 60 &
                  (is.na(first_obs) | first_obs >= start_date),

    # CHECK 2: last observation falls at the end of a school year (May–Aug),
    #          so the notes didn't stop early
    check_last_obs = !is.na(last_obs) & month(last_obs) %in% 5:8,

    # CHECK 3: school year in which kindergarten ended matches the current group
    end_year          = if_else(month(last_obs) >= 9, year(last_obs) + 1, year(last_obs)),
    expected_end_year = ref_year - (curr_year_group - 3), 
    check_group       = !is.na(end_year) & end_year == expected_end_year,

    all_checks_ok = check_start & check_last_obs & check_group
  )

# how many pupils pass each check
kindergarten_checked |>
  summarise(n_pupils = n(),
            across(c(check_start, check_last_obs, check_group, all_checks_ok),
                  ~sum(.x, na.rm = TRUE)))

# which pupils fail, and why
kindergarten_checked |>
  filter(!all_checks_ok | is.na(all_checks_ok)) |>
  select(pupil, curr_year_group, birth_date, start_date,
         first_obs, last_obs, days_after_4th_bday, end_year, expected_end_year,
         check_start, check_last_obs, check_group)
```
## Interpertation
The table above shows that there are 25 pupils who did not pass the checks. 
Firstly, of these pupils, 18 are currently in grade 8. These all failed the check
verifying whether the last observation in grade 1/2 was in July or August. The
last observation of these pupils were all recorded in december. So either their
observations got lost or were not stored correctly. As we are examining
development in grades 3:4, we could remove pupils in grade 7 all together to
ensure that each grade is represented by an equal amount of students. Secondly,
two pupils from grade 5 failed because of NAs and one because the first observation
was before the start_date. To ensure we have reliable information these pupils 
will also not be included in the analysis. The remaining pupils who failed the 
checks were in group 3 and 4. One because if NAs and in every other case because
the pupils should have left kindergarten a year earlier than their current group
implies. This could be explained if these pupils had to redo year 3 or 4. These 
pupils will also not be included in further analysis. Leaving us with a total 
sample size of N = 79. 


```{r}
# asked claude how to visualise the distribution 
kg_plot <- kindergarten_checked |>
  filter(curr_year_group %in% 3:6, all_checks_ok) |>
  mutate(kindergarten_years = time_length(interval(start_date, make_date(end_year, 9, 1)), "years"))


kg_plot |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean = mean(kindergarten_years),
            sd = sd(kindergarten_years),
            min = min(kindergarten_years),
            median = median(kindergarten_years),
            max = max(kindergarten_years))


ggplot(kg_plot, aes(x = kindergarten_years)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1/12, colour = "white", fill =  "#01665e") +
  labs(x = "Time in kindergarten (years)",
       y = "Number of pupils",
       title = "Distribution of time spent in Kindergarten by the selected pupils", 
       subtitle = "N = 79") 

```

To operationalize the cognitive, social-emotional and executive development of the pupils, we obtain the scores from the observations from Group1/2 from selected domains. Below are the domains we used to measure each of the three functions. In this analysis, we assume that each objective carries the same weight in measuring the developmental function.

|      *Cognitive*        |   *Social-emotional* |  *Executive development*  |
|:-----------------------:|:--------------------:|:-------------------------:|
|Auditory development     |Society               |Balancing                  |
|Numbers                  |Emotional competencies|Engagement                 |
|Interactive language use |Empathy               |Emotional competencies     |
|Knowledge                |Self and others       |Impulse control            |
|Process                  |The space around you  |Moral competencies         |
|Play                     |Social initiative     |Task focus and independence|
|Playing                  |Social autonomy       |                           |
|Counting and number sense|Social competencies   |                           |
|Counting and numbers     |Social flexibility    |                           |
|Visual development       |Rough-and-tumble play |                           |
|                         |Well-being            |                           |

Firstly, the 79 pupils who pass all checks are saved in a table. The observations file is imported in the correct format, this time to extract the domain information from it. Only the rows with observations from the selected pupils are retained. Scores are re-coded to values from 0-3.

```{r}
  filter(Leerling %in% pupils_ok$pupil,

           "Spelen",

           "Tellen en getallen",
           "Visuele ontwikkeling",
           "De samenleving",
           "Emotionele competenties",
           "Inlevingsvermogen",
           "Jezelf en de ander",
           "Ruimte om je heen",
           "Sociaal initiatief",
           "Sociale autonomie",
           "Sociale competenties",
           "Sociale flexibiliteit",
           "Stoeispelen",
           "Welbevinden",
           "Betrokkenheid",

observation_selection

```

We check if there are any missing values in the dataset, and find that 115 values are missing from Scores. As previously, these rows will not be included in the analysis to maintain reliability and consistency. However, we check if removing these rows led to dropping any pupils altogether, and we find that this is not the case.

```{r}
#check if any values are NAs = 115 NAs in score
sum(is.na(observation_selection))

#store rows with NAs in different table

observation_selection_nas

observation_selection

length(pupils_dropped)

```

We create a column with the development function, in which, each domain will be identified with their respective label of the three functions it belongs to (cognitive, social-emotional, executive).

```{r}

observation_selection <- observation_selection |>
  mutate(
    development_function = case_when(
     Domein %in% c(
    "Auditieve ontwikkeling",
    "Getallen",
    "Kennis",
    "Proces",
    "Spel",
    "Spelen",
    "Tellen en getalbegrip",
    "Tellen en getallen",
    "Visuele ontwikkeling"
    ) ~ "Cognitive",

      Domein %in% c(
        "De samenleving",
        "Inlevingsvermogen",
        "Interactief taalgebruik",
        "Jezelf en de ander",
        "Ruimte om je heen",
        "Sociaal initiatief",
        "Sociale autonomie",
        "Sociale competenties",
        "Sociale flexibiliteit",
        "Stoeispelen",
        "Welbevinden"
        ) ~ "Social-emotional",

      Domein %in% c(
        "Balanceren",
        "Betrokkenheid",
        "Emotionele competenties",
        "Impulsbeheersing",
        "Morele competenties",
        "Taakgerichtheid en zelfstandigheid"
        ) ~ "Executive",

      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  )
observation_selection

```

First, we calculate the elapsed time and six-month interval for every observation.

Some pupils have observations recorded at different times of the year. By calculating the elapsed time relative to each pupil's own start date, we will be able to align the observations by 'time spent in kindergarten', rather than by calendar year.

```{r}
#Calculate the elapsed time since starting kindergarten for every observation

scores_over_time <- observation_selection |>
  left_join(
    kindergarten_checked |> select(pupil, start_date),
    by = c("Leerling" = "pupil")
  ) |>
  mutate(
    time_in_kindergarten = as.numeric(Datum - start_date) / 365.25,
    time_period = floor(time_in_kindergarten * 2) / 2
  )
scores_over_time
```

We calculate the average score for each objective, per pupil, per six-month interval. We group observations into six month intervals, to calculate comparable average scores for each pupil and developmental function at successive stages in their kindergarten time.

Then, we calculate the average of the objectives scores per developmental function. We use the average of the objective scores to ensure that each objective received equal weight. 'n_domain' records the number of objectives contributing to each function score. We can then investigate if recorded scores tend to improve as time in kindergarten increases.

```{r}

# Average score per objective, per pupil, per six-month interval
domain_scores_6_months <- scores_over_time |>
  group_by(Leerling, time_period, development_function, Domein) |>
  summarise(
    domain_score = mean(Score, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_observations = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
domain_scores_6_months

# Average objective scores per developmental function
function_scores_6_months <- domain_scores_6_months |>
  filter(!is.na(development_function)) |>
  group_by(Leerling, time_period, development_function) |>
  summarise(
    function_score = mean(domain_score, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_domain = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
function_scores_6_months

```
The plot below addresses the question "How do developmental function scores tend to change as the time since kindergarten entry increases?"

Each thin, grey line represents one pupil, showing for each function how average scores change across every 6 months spent in kindergarten. The blue trend line reflects the overall relationship between time spent in kindergarten and the recorded scores for each function across all pupils. When it rises, the function scores tend to be higher at later intervals (longer period spent in kindergarten).

```{r}

ggplot(
  function_scores_6_months,
  aes(x = time_period, y = function_score, group = Leerling)
) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_smooth(
    aes(group = 1),
    method = "loess",
    se = TRUE,
    colour = "blue"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ development_function, ncol = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 4, by = 0.5)) +
  labs(
    x = "Years since starting kindergarten",
    y = "Average developmental score",
    title = "Developmental scores over time in kindergarten"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
  
```
We calculate the mean, standard deviation and the number of pupils contributing to each time period for each function, to see whether scores improve overtime. 

```{r}
interval_summary <- function_scores_6_months |>
  group_by(time_period, development_function) |>
  summarise(
    mean_score = mean(function_score, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_score = sd(function_score, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_pupils = n_distinct(Leerling[!is.na(function_score)]),
    se = sd_score / sqrt(n_pupils),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

interval_summary

```

Next, we visualize how average developmental function scores change over time in kindergarten. Larger points indicate that more pupil observations contributed data.

```{r}

ggplot(
  interval_summary,
  aes(x = time_period, y = mean_score)
) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(aes(size = n_pupils)) +
  facet_wrap(~ development_function, ncol = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 4, by = 0.5)) +
  labs(
    x = "Years since starting kindergarten",
    y = "Mean developmental score",
    size = "Number of pupils",
    title = "Average developmental scores by time in kindergarten",
    subtitle = "Error bars show approximate 95% confidence intervals"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

```
Finally, we fitted separate mixed-effect models for each function, and adjusted the p-values to account for testing multiple functions.

As shown below, the results suggest that all three functions have a statistically significant positive relationship with kindergarten duration (p values where p<0.05). Cognition has the largest estimated increase (0.195 per 6 months), followed by social-emotional (0.171) and executive development (0.150).

``` {r}
library(lme4)
library(dplyr)
library(lmerTest)

model_results <- function_scores_6_months |>
  filter(!is.na(function_score), !is.na(time_period)) |>
  group_by(development_function) |>
  group_modify(~ {
    model <- lmer(
      function_score ~ time_period + (1 | Leerling),
      data = .x
    )

    tibble(
      estimate = fixef(model)["time_period"],
      p_value = summary(model)$coefficients[
        "time_period", "Pr(>|t|)"
      ]
    )
  }) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(
    p_adjusted = p.adjust(p_value, method = "BH")
  )

model_results

```

# Conclusion RQ1 - Kindergarten duration and developmental functioning

The above analysis suggests that the three development functions (cognitive, social-emotional and executive development), as measured by pupil's scores in their observations, tend to increase the longer the pupils stay in kindergarten. For every additional 6 months, cognitive function increased by almost 0.2 points, while social-emotional by 0.17 and executive development by 0.15.

The model results showed statistical significance between kindergarten duration and each developmental function, meaning that these relationships are unlikely to be due to random variation alone. 

Overall, the findings show that pupils tend to attain higher developmental scores as their time spent in kindergarten increases. It is not proven that this is a causal relationship.


# RQ1 - Kindergarten duration and functioning in Years 3 & 4

To address the second part of the RQ1, which questions how the duration of kindergarten affects functioning in Years 3 & 4, we first look at the cito test scores from these pupils.

Created by Cito (Central Institute for Test Development), these tests measure primary school pupils' academic progress throughout the years and help guide their secondary school placement. Here, we will use these test results to reflect their levels of academic achievement in grades 3 and 4. 

For our analysis, we retain only pupils in Grades 3 and 4 across all cohorts (2028-2031), and restrict the dataset to pupils included in our for kindergarten analysis. We also select only the tests administered in Grades 3 and 4, excluding tests relevant for later grades (Grade 5 and 6) to ensure consistency and comparability across analyses. We also change performance band "I+" to "I" and "V-" to "V", as there was only one value of each in the dataset.

```{r}

cito <- bind_rows(
  read_excel(here::here("data", "Cito_UvA_EN.xlsx"), sheet = "CLASS_2028"),
  read_excel(here::here("data", "Cito_UvA_EN.xlsx"), sheet = "CLASS_2029"),
  read_excel(here::here("data", "Cito_UvA_EN.xlsx"), sheet = "CLASS_2030"),
  read_excel(here::here("data", "Cito_UvA_EN.xlsx"), sheet = "CLASS_2031")
  ) %>%
  select(-"Performance band value", -"Ability score", -"Cohort year") %>%
  mutate(
    across(c(1:3, 5:6), as.character),
    across(4, as.numeric),
    `Performance band` = recode(
      `Performance band`,
      "I+" = "I",
      "V-" = "V"
    )
  ) %>%
  filter(
    Name %in% pupils_ok$pupil,
    Grade %in% c("Grade 3", "Grade 4"),
    Test %in% c(
      "TMT",
      "Mathematics",
      "Spelling – Non-verbs",
      "Reading Comprehension"
    ))

```
We must check if the data have any missing values, and especially if any pupils from the kindergarten duration data are not included in the cito data.

```{r}

# Names in function_scores_6_months that are missing from cito data
missing_students <- setdiff(
  unique(function_scores_6_months$Leerling),
  unique(cito$Name)
)

missing_students
length(missing_students)

#33 NAs
sum(is.na(cito)) 

```
25 students will be excluded from the analysis linking kindergarten to Cito performance because their Cito scores are unavailable. This reduces the sample size of pupils to 54.

Below we find that 17 cito scores and 16 performance band values are missing. We inspect in which rows these are, and find that all missing performance band values coincide with missing test scores, while one additional test score is missing despite having a performance band value. We therefore remove the rows with missing data and check whether this results in any additional pupils being excluded. We find that this is not the case, the number of excluded pupils remains 25.

```{r}
#which columns in cito have missing values
colSums(is.na(cito))

#which rows in score and performance band have missing values
which(is.na(cito$Score))
which(is.na(cito$`Performance band`))

#drop rows with missing values
cito <- drop_na(cito)

#check again if any columns have missing values
colSums(is.na(cito))

#check if pupils in fuctnions data still match or if more were dropped
missing_students2 <- setdiff(
  unique(function_scores_6_months$Leerling),
  unique(cito$Name)
)
missing_students2 #still 25 missing, no new pupils dropped
length(missing_students2)

```
We join the Cito data with the kindergarten duration data, matching by pupil's names.

```{r}
cito_analysis <- cito |>
  left_join(
    kindergarten_checked |>
      select(pupil, kindergarten_years),
    by = c("Name" = "pupil")
  )

#check that every pupil in cito has a matched kindergarten duration value
sum(is.na(cito_analysis$kindergarten_years))
```
Dividing kindergarten duration into six-month intervals here results in groups with too few pupils to reliably compare them. Since the average (mean) time in kindergarten is approximately two years, we divide the pupils into two groups: those who spent two years or less in kindergarten, and those who spent more. The groups now allow for a more practical comparison of their cito scores.

```{r}
mean(cito_analysis$kindergarten_years)

cito_analysis <- cito_analysis |>
  mutate(
    duration_group = if_else(
      kindergarten_years <= 2,
      "2 years or less",
      "more than 2 years"
    )
  )
 
cito_analysis |>
  distinct(Name, duration_group) |>
  count(duration_group)

```
Below we calculate the number and percentage of pupils in each performance band to compare the distribution of the bands between the two duration groups.

```{r}
band_summary <- cito_analysis |>
  filter(!is.na(`Performance band`)) |>
  distinct(Name, Test, `Assessment period`, duration_group,
           `Performance band`) |>
  group_by(Test, duration_group, `Performance band`) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  group_by(Test, duration_group) |>
  mutate(
    percentage = 100 * n / sum(n)
  ) |>
  ungroup()

band_summary

```

The plot below compares the distribution of the performance bands per test between pupils who spent two years or less in kindergarten, and those who spent more. The results combine all cohorts and assessment periods together.

```{r}

ggplot(
  band_summary,
  aes(
    x = duration_group,
    y = percentage,
    fill = `Performance band`
  )
) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  facet_wrap(~ Test) +
  labs(
    x = "Kindergarten duration",
    y = "Percentage of pupils tested",
    fill = "Performance band",
    title = "Cito performance bands by kindergarten duration",
    subtitle = "(All cohorts and assessment periods combined)"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
    strip.background = element_rect(
      fill = "#EFE2BA"
  ))
```

According to the above visualization, spending longer (more than two years) in kindergarten does not have a consistent advantage in functioning in Years 3 & 4 in terms of Cito test scores. Pupils with longer kindergarten periods show higher performance in TMT, and, to a lesser extent, spelling (non-verbs). However, there is no clear advantage in reading comprehension, while mathematics shows a lowered number of pupils in the top-performing band for longer kindergarten periods. These patterns suggest that any association between kindergarten duration and Cito test performance are likely subject-specific rather than general.

# RQ2: Teaching focus on Year 3 objectives

*What effects does a teaching focus on learning objectives aligned with Years 3
and 4 have on pupils' academic achievement and subsequent educational pathways?*

## Approach in short

The school has selected 15 learning goals that pupils should reach **before**
they start group 3 (file `Selected learning goals.xlsx`, sheet 2). For RQ2 we
ask: do pupils who mastered more of these goals by the end of kindergarten do
better in Year 3 and 4?

| Role | Variable | Source file |
|---|---|---|
| Predictor | % of the 15 Year 3 goals mastered at the end of kindergarten | `Observaties_groep_1_2.xlsx` |
| Outcome: achievement | Cito scores in Year 3 (mid and end) and Year 4 (end) for Mathematics, TMT (reading speed) and Spelling | `Cito_UvA_EN.xlsx` |
| Outcome: falling behind | Cito performance band IV or V (bottom 40% nationally) | `Cito_UvA_EN.xlsx` |
| Outcome: keeping up with lessons | % of test goals passed in the school's own maths tests, Year 3 and 4 | `UvA_testresults_math.xlsx` |
| Outcome: pathway | Academic support needed (started or waiting list) and received in Year 3 | `Support interventions_care team.xlsx` |
| Controls | Age at the start of Year 3, cohort (current group) | `Pupils.xlsx` |

The steps below are: (1) select pupils, (2) identify the Year 3 goals,
(3) clean the observation scores, (4) compute mastery per pupil, (5) build the
Cito and support outcomes, (6) combine everything into one dataset, and
(7) analyse it.

## 1. Pupils

We start from the same pupils as RQ1 (`pupil_selection`, groups 3-7). Unlike
RQ1, pupils who failed the kindergarten checks are **kept**, because repeating
a year is itself a possible RQ2 outcome.

The files do not share an ID: the pupil file uses `Pupil 002`, the support file
`Leerling 018` and the maths file just `7`. Pupil **names** are unique in the
pupil file and appear in every file, so names are used to link the files.
`str_squish()` removes accidental double or trailing spaces so that names match
exactly.

```{r rq2 pupils}
rq2_pupils <- pupil_selection |>
  mutate(pupil = str_squish(pupil))   # "Anna  Peters " -> "Anna Peters"
```

## 2. The Year 3 goals

Sheet 2 of `Selected learning goals.xlsx` ("Goals before grade one") lists the
15 goals the school listed as important for a successful start in Year 3.
Each goal has a code (e.g. `TG11.2_E2`) in the same format as the column
`Leerpadcode` in the observations, which is how goals and observations are
linked. The sheet has three title rows above the header, hence `skip = 3`.

Two other options were checked and rejected:

- `Vaktype` has a category "check", but it only covers world orientation,
  crafts and performing arts, not the Year 3 goals.
- `Leercode` is a legacy column: it is filled for almost all rows until
  2021/22 and empty from 2024/25 onwards (the school changed its recording
  system). It is therefore not used, and it is skipped when importing.

```{r rq2 goals}
year3_goals <- read_xlsx(here::here("data", "Selected learning goals.xlsx"),
                         sheet = 2, skip = 3) |>
  select(goal_no = 1, goal = 2, code = 3) |>   # rename the three columns
  filter(!is.na(code)) |>                      # drop empty rows
  mutate(code = str_squish(code))

# number of goals, and share of goal codes that appear in the observations
nrow(year3_goals)
mean(year3_goals$code %in% observation_selection$Leerpadcode)
```

All 15 goal codes appear in the observations (share = 1).

## 3. Cleaning the observation scores

Teachers score each goal on a scale of 0-4, which in practice is 0-3. The score
distribution showed:

- mostly 0, 1, 2 and 3;
- a few half scores (1.5, 2.5, 3.5), which are kept;
- 406 scores of 4, which are recoded to 3 (the highest level used in practice);
- three impossible scores (5 and 22), which are set to missing (`NA`).

```{r rq2 score cleaning}
obs_rq2 <- observation_selection |>
  mutate(Leerling = str_squish(Leerling),
         Score = case_when(Score == 4 ~ 3,          # 4 -> 3
                           Score > 4 ~ NA_real_,   # 5 and 22 -> missing
                           TRUE ~ Score))     # everything else unchanged
```

## 4. Mastery per pupil (the predictor)

A goal is usually observed several times during kindergarten. We want to know
where a pupil **ended up** before Year 3, so for each pupil and goal only the
**most recent** score is kept (`arrange(desc(Datum))` puts the latest date
first, `slice(1)` keeps that row).

A goal counts as **mastered** when that last score is 3 (the highest level).
Then, per pupil:

- `n_goals_observed`: how many of the 15 goals were observed at all;
- `pct_mastered`: mastered goals as a % of all 15 goals (main measure; a goal
  that was never observed counts as not mastered);
- `pct_mastered_2`: the same, but with score 2 or higher counting as mastered
  (robustness check);
- `pct_of_observed`: mastered goals as a % of the goals that were observed
  (robustness check for pupils with incomplete records).

```{r rq2 mastery}
# last score per pupil per Year 3 goal
last_scores <- obs_rq2 |>
  filter(Leerpadcode %in% year3_goals$code, !is.na(Score)) |>
  group_by(Leerling, Leerpadcode) |>
  arrange(desc(Datum)) |>
  slice(1) |>
  ungroup()

# summary per pupil
mastery <- last_scores |>
  group_by(Leerling) |>
  summarise(n_goals_observed = n(),
            n_mastered = sum(Score >= 3),
            n_mastered_2 = sum(Score >= 2)) |>
  mutate(pct_mastered = n_mastered   / nrow(year3_goals) * 100,
         pct_mastered_2 = n_mastered_2 / nrow(year3_goals) * 100,
         pct_of_observed = n_mastered   / n_goals_observed * 100)
```

### Table 2 requested by the school

I believe this is what the school asked for:
how many goals were designated as important for Year 3, what % of these pupils have mastered on average when starting Year 3, and the lowest and highest values across pupils.

```{r rq2 table 2}
mastery |>
  summarise(n_goals = nrow(year3_goals),
            n_pupils = n(),
            mean_pct = mean(pct_mastered),
            min_pct = min(pct_mastered),
            max_pct = max(pct_mastered),
            mean_pct_ge2 = mean(pct_mastered_2))
```

**Interpretation.** On average pupils mastered about two thirds (68%) of the 15
goals by the start of Year 3, with large differences between pupils (from 13%
to 100%). With the looser definition (score 2 or higher), the average is 83%.

### How complete are the records per group?

If a pupil's record is incomplete, the main measure underestimates their
mastery. This table compares the groups.

```{r rq2 completeness}
mastery |>
  left_join(rq2_pupils, by = c("Leerling" = "pupil")) |>
  group_by(curr_year_group) |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean_goals_observed = mean(n_goals_observed),
            mean_pct            = mean(pct_mastered),
            mean_pct_observed   = mean(pct_of_observed))
```

**Interpretation.** Groups 3-6 have nearly complete records (13.5-14.7 of the
15 goals observed). Group 7 has on average only about 10 goals observed, and
their mastery drops from 68% (of observed goals) to 46% (of all goals): the gap
comes from missing observations, not lower mastery. This matches the RQ1
finding that their kindergarten records stop in December. **Group 7 is
therefore excluded from the outcome analysis.**

## 5a. Outcomes: Cito results

The Cito workbook has one sheet per cohort (`CLASS_2028` to `CLASS_2031`). They
are read in and stacked into one table. Some cleaning is needed:

- **Column names** are made lower case with underscores
  (`Assessment period` -> `assessment_period`).
- **`assessment_period`** holds two things, e.g. `"end 2022-2023"`. It is split
  into `period` (mid/end) and `school_year`.
- **Which score?** The Cito file has four related columns:

| Column | What it is | Comparable between... | Used? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `score` | Cito's ability scale (*vaardigheidsscore*): correct answers converted to one long scale that runs through primary school, like a height chart. For TMT it is the number of words read correctly in three minutes. | **Moments** within the same test (it rises with age), so progress can be computed. **Not** between tests: maths and spelling have their own scales. | **Yes**: main outcome, always per test. |
| `ability_score` | A relative score (0-5): the pupil's position compared with pupils nationally. Its mean is about 2.2 in every grade, and it rises from band V (mean 1.1) to band I (mean 4.2). | Between tests and grades. | **No**: missing for 82% of the Grade 3 results. |
| `performance_band` | National norm group, I-V, each 20% of pupils: I = top 20%, V = bottom 20%. Based on the score, using the cut-offs in the "Score ranges" sheet. "I+" is treated as I. | Between tests and moments. | **Yes**: band IV or V counts as *behind*. |
| `performance_band_value` | Meant as the band as a number, but inconsistent (band I has values 2.0-5.0). | Not reliable. | **No**. |

  Band V is by far the most common band at this school, so being "behind"
  nationally is common here; this is important context for the results.

- **Falling behind.** `performance_band` (I-V) compares a pupil with national
  norms: I is the top 20%, V the bottom 20%. "I+" is treated as I. Band IV or V
  counts as *behind*. The column `performance_band_value` is inconsistent and
  is not used.
- **Tests.** Only Mathematics, TMT (reading speed) and Spelling (non-verbs) are
  used, because these were tested in Grade 3 in every school year. Reading
  Comprehension is missing in Grade 3 for two of the four years.

```{r rq2 cito}
cito <- map_dfr(c("CLASS_2028", "CLASS_2029", "CLASS_2030", "CLASS_2031"),
                ~ read_xlsx(here::here("data", "Cito_UvA_EN.xlsx"),
                            sheet = .x, col_types = "text")) |>
  rename_with(~ .x |> str_to_lower() |> str_replace_all("[^a-z0-9]+", "_") |>
                str_remove("_$")) |>
  mutate(name = str_squish(name))

cito_clean <- cito |>
  separate_wider_delim(assessment_period, delim = " ",
                       names = c("period", "school_year"),
                       too_many = "merge") |>
  mutate(grade_num = parse_number(grade),                 # "Grade 3" -> 3
         score     = as.numeric(score),
         band      = str_remove(performance_band, "[+-]"), # "I+" -> "I"
         behind    = if_else(is.na(band), NA, band %in% c("IV", "V"))) |>
  filter(test %in% c("Mathematics", "TMT", "Spelling – Non-verbs"))

# check: number of missing scores per test and grade
cito_clean |> count(test, grade, missing_score = is.na(score))
```

### Repeaters

A pupil with results for the **same grade in two different school years** has
repeated that year. This is checked here because repeating is a possible
pathway outcome.

```{r rq2 repeaters}
repeaters <- cito_clean |>
  group_by(name, grade_num) |>
  summarise(n_years = n_distinct(school_year), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(name) |>
  summarise(repeated_year = any(n_years > 1))

repeaters |> count(repeated_year)
```

Only one pupil repeated a year. That is too few to analyse, so repeating is
reported descriptively but not used as an outcome.

### One row per pupil

The Cito data has one row per pupil per test per moment. For the analysis we
need one row per pupil, with a column for each test and moment (e.g.
`score_math_g3_mid` = maths score in the middle of Year 3). `pivot_wider()`
does this. For the repeater, only the **first attempt** is used
(`arrange(school_year)` then `slice(1)`), because that reflects the level they
started Year 3 with.

`math_progress` is the gain in maths from the middle of Year 3 to the end of
Year 4.

```{r rq2 cito outcomes}
outcomes <- cito_clean |>
  filter(grade_num == 3 | (grade_num == 4 & period == "end")) |>
  group_by(name, test, grade_num, period) |>
  arrange(school_year) |>
  slice(1) |>                                   # first attempt only
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(moment = paste0("g", grade_num, "_", period),   # e.g. "g3_mid"
         test   = recode(test, "Mathematics" = "math", "TMT" = "tmt",
                         "Spelling – Non-verbs" = "spelling")) |>
  select(name, test, moment, score, behind) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = c(test, moment),
              values_from = c(score, behind)) |>
  mutate(math_progress = score_math_g4_end - score_math_g3_mid) |>
  left_join(repeaters, by = "name")
```

## 5b. Outcomes: support in Year 3

The support file records each referral with the school year (e.g. `2324` =
2023/24), but not the pupil's group at that time. The group is worked out from
the current group:

> group at that time = current group - (2026 - start year of that school year)

For example, a pupil now in group 5 was in group 3 in 2024/25.

Choices made:

- Only support that actually **started** is counted (`Started? = Yes`);
  referrals on the waiting list are not.
- **Academic support** means remedial teaching, a language group or 1:1 speech
  therapy. Motor therapy and behaviour support are less related to being ready in Year 3.
- The file covers 2023/24 to 2025/26, so Year 3 support is only known for
  pupils now in groups 4-6. For them, a pupil **without a record** is assumed
  to have received **no support**.

```{r rq2 support}
support <- read_xlsx(here::here("data", "Support interventions_care team.xlsx"),
                     skip = 1) |>                 # first row is not the header
  rename_with(~ .x |> str_to_lower() |> str_replace_all("[^a-z0-9]+", "_") |>
                str_remove("_$")) |>
  mutate(student_name = str_squish(student_name))

academic_types <- c("Remedial teaching", "Language group", "1:1 speech therapy")

support_y3 <- support |>
  filter(!is.na(student_name), !is.na(school_yr), started == "Yes") |>
  inner_join(rq2_pupils |> select(pupil, curr_year_group),
             by = c("student_name" = "pupil")) |>
  mutate(start_year    = 2000 + school_yr %/% 100,   # 2324 -> 2023
         group_at_time = curr_year_group - (2026 - start_year)) |>
  filter(group_at_time == 3) |>                      # support in Year 3 only
  group_by(student_name) |>
  summarise(n_support_y3          = n(),
            n_academic_support_y3 = sum(support_type %in% academic_types))
```

## 6. Analysis dataset

Everything is joined into one table with **one row per pupil** in groups 4-6:

- group 3 is left out because they have no Year 3 Cito results yet;
- group 7 is left out because their kindergarten records are incomplete.

Two control variables are added:

- **age at the start of Year 3** (Year 3 starts on 1 September of
  2026 - (current group - 3));
- **winter birthday** (born October-December), a group the school specifically
  asked about.

```{r rq2 analysis data}
rq2_data <- rq2_pupils |>
  select(pupil, curr_year_group, birth_date, start_date) |>
  filter(curr_year_group %in% 4:6) |>
  left_join(mastery, by = c("pupil" = "Leerling")) |>
  left_join(outcomes, by = c("pupil" = "name")) |>
  left_join(support_y3, by = c("pupil" = "student_name")) |>
  mutate(
    year3_start = make_date(2026 - (curr_year_group - 3), 9, 1),
    age_year3   = time_length(interval(birth_date, year3_start), "years"),
    winter_bday = month(birth_date) %in% 10:12,
    across(c(n_support_y3, n_academic_support_y3), ~ replace_na(.x, 0)),
    any_academic_support_y3 = n_academic_support_y3 > 0
  )

# pupils per group
rq2_data |> count(curr_year_group)

# number of pupils with a value for each variable
rq2_data |>
  summarise(across(c(pct_mastered, score_math_g3_mid, score_tmt_g3_mid,
                     score_spelling_g3_mid, math_progress,
                     any_academic_support_y3, age_year3),
                   ~ sum(!is.na(.x)))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "n_non_missing")
```

**Interpretation.** The analysis sample has 60 pupils (30 in group 4, 16 in
group 5, 14 in group 6). Mastery and the Year 3 mid scores are available for
58-59 of them. `math_progress` is only available for 30 pupils, because
current group 4 has not taken the end-of-Year-4 test yet.

## 7. Analysis

### 7a. Lower vs higher mastery

As a first, simple comparison, pupils are split at the median of
`pct_mastered` into a "lower" and a "higher" mastery group.

```{r rq2 descriptives}
rq2_data <- rq2_data |>
  mutate(mastery_group = if_else(pct_mastered >= median(pct_mastered, na.rm = TRUE),
                                 "higher", "lower"))

rq2_data |>
  filter(!is.na(mastery_group)) |>
  group_by(mastery_group) |>
  summarise(n                = n(),
            mean_mastery     = mean(pct_mastered),
            math_g3_mid      = mean(score_math_g3_mid, na.rm = TRUE),
            tmt_g3_mid       = mean(score_tmt_g3_mid, na.rm = TRUE),
            spelling_g3_mid  = mean(score_spelling_g3_mid, na.rm = TRUE),
            pct_behind_math  = mean(behind_math_g3_mid, na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
            pct_behind_tmt   = mean(behind_tmt_g3_mid, na.rm = TRUE) * 100,
            pct_acad_support = mean(any_academic_support_y3) * 100,
            math_progress    = mean(math_progress, na.rm = TRUE))
```

**Interpretation.** Pupils with higher mastery score higher on all three tests
in the middle of Year 3. They are also much less often behind: in maths,
roughly 4 in 10 pupils with higher mastery are in band IV/V, compared with
roughly 8 in 10 pupils with lower mastery.

### 7b. Mastery and Year 3 scores

Each dot is a pupil; the black line is a linear fit with its 95% confidence
band.

```{r rq2 plots}
rq2_data |>
  select(pupil, curr_year_group, pct_mastered,
         Mathematics = score_math_g3_mid, TMT = score_tmt_g3_mid,
         Spelling = score_spelling_g3_mid) |>
  pivot_longer(c(Mathematics, TMT, Spelling), names_to = "test", values_to = "score") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = pct_mastered, y = score)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = factor(curr_year_group))) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, colour = "black") +
  facet_wrap(~ test, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "% of Year 3 goals mastered at end of kindergarten",
       y = "Cito score, Year 3 mid",
       colour = "Current group")
```

### 7c. Regression

A linear regression estimates how much the Year 3 score changes per percentage
point of mastery, while holding age at the start of Year 3 and cohort constant.
Cohort (`factor(curr_year_group)`) is included because each group took the
Year 3 test in a different school year. Pupils with a missing value on any
variable in a model are left out of that model.

```{r rq2 regression}
model_math     <- lm(score_math_g3_mid     ~ pct_mastered + age_year3 + factor(curr_year_group), data = rq2_data)
model_tmt      <- lm(score_tmt_g3_mid      ~ pct_mastered + age_year3 + factor(curr_year_group), data = rq2_data)
model_spelling <- lm(score_spelling_g3_mid ~ pct_mastered + age_year3 + factor(curr_year_group), data = rq2_data)

summary(model_math)
summary(model_tmt)
summary(model_spelling)
```

**Interpretation.**

- **Mathematics:** each extra 10 percentage points of mastery goes with about
  11 points higher on the Year 3 mid Cito maths score (b = 1.07 per point,
  p < .001, n = 57).
- **Spelling:** about 12 points higher per 10 percentage points (b = 1.21,
  p = .002, n = 56).
- **TMT (reading speed):** a positive but not significant relation (b = 0.12,
  p = .13). TMT differs mainly between cohorts, and a few very high scores
  influence the line.
- The models explain about a third of the differences between pupils
  (R² ≈ .34-.36). Age at the start of Year 3 is negatively related to scores,
  but not significantly.

### 7d. Robustness checks

Do the maths results depend on the choices made above? Three checks:

1. a looser definition of mastery (score 2 or higher);
2. mastery as a % of the goals that were actually observed;
3. leaving out pupils who are far from the regression line (standardised
   residual larger than 2.5).

For check 3 the model is first refitted on the pupils without missing values,
so that the residuals line up with the right pupils.

```{r rq2 robustness}
# 1. looser mastery definition
summary(lm(score_math_g3_mid ~ pct_mastered_2  + age_year3 + factor(curr_year_group), data = rq2_data))

# 2. % of observed goals
summary(lm(score_math_g3_mid ~ pct_of_observed + age_year3 + factor(curr_year_group), data = rq2_data))

# 3. without extreme pupils
rq2_math <- rq2_data |>
  filter(!is.na(score_math_g3_mid), !is.na(pct_mastered), !is.na(age_year3))
model_math_cc <- lm(score_math_g3_mid ~ pct_mastered + age_year3 + factor(curr_year_group), data = rq2_math)
rq2_trim <- rq2_math |> filter(abs(rstandard(model_math_cc)) < 2.5)
summary(lm(score_math_g3_mid ~ pct_mastered + age_year3 + factor(curr_year_group), data = rq2_trim))

# model diagnostics for the main maths model
par(mfrow = c(2, 2)); plot(model_math); par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

**Interpretation.** The maths result holds in all three checks: with a looser
definition of mastery the relation is weaker but still significant (b = 1.40,
p = .006); as a % of observed goals it is almost identical (b = 1.09,
p < .001); and without extreme pupils it is the same (b = 1.09, p < .001). The
diagnostic plots show some right skew in the residuals (a few pupils score much
higher than predicted), but no influential outliers and roughly constant
variance.

### 7e. Later moments: end of Year 3, end of Year 4 and progress

The analysis above used the middle of Year 3. Here the same model is applied to
later moments, to see whether the relation with mastery lasts. One row per
outcome: `b` is the change in score per percentage point of mastery (controlling
for age at the start of Year 3 and cohort).

- End of Year 4 scores and maths progress (mid Year 3 to end Year 4) are only
  available for current groups 5 and 6 (about 30 pupils).

```{r rq2 later moments}
# helper: fit the model for one outcome and keep the mastery row
mastery_effect <- function(outcome, data = rq2_data) {
  f <- as.formula(paste(outcome, "~ pct_mastered + age_year3 + factor(curr_year_group)"))
  m <- lm(f, data = data)
  co <- summary(m)$coefficients["pct_mastered", ]
  tibble(outcome = outcome,
         b       = round(co[["Estimate"]], 2),
         se      = round(co[["Std. Error"]], 2),
         p       = signif(co[["Pr(>|t|)"]], 2),
         n       = nobs(m),
         r2      = round(summary(m)$r.squared, 2))
}

c("score_math_g3_mid",     "score_math_g3_end",     "score_math_g4_end",
  "score_spelling_g3_mid", "score_spelling_g3_end", "score_spelling_g4_end",
  "score_tmt_g3_mid",      "score_tmt_g3_end",      "score_tmt_g4_end",
  "math_progress") |>
  map_dfr(mastery_effect)
```

**Interpretation.** The relation between mastery and maths lasts: it is
significant in the middle of Year 3 (b = 1.07), at the end of Year 3 (b = 0.86)
and at the end of Year 4 (b = 1.40, n = 29). For spelling it lasts through Year 3
(b = 0.78 at the end of Year 3); at the end of Year 4 it is still positive but not
significant, which may be due to the small sample (n = 29). For reading speed
(TMT) there is no relation at any moment. Pupils with higher mastery do **not**
make faster progress in maths from mid Year 3 to end Year 4 (b = 0.24, p = .30):
they start Year 3 at a higher level and keep that lead, but the gap does not grow.

### 7f. Falling behind over time

Share of pupils in band IV or V, per test and moment, for pupils with lower and
higher mastery.

```{r rq2 behind over time}
rq2_data |>
  filter(!is.na(mastery_group)) |>
  select(mastery_group, starts_with("behind_")) |>
  pivot_longer(-mastery_group,
               names_to = c("test", "moment"),
               names_pattern = "behind_(.*)_(g\\d_.*)",
               values_to = "behind") |>
  filter(!is.na(behind)) |>
  group_by(test, moment, mastery_group) |>
  summarise(n = n(), pct_behind = round(mean(behind) * 100), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = mastery_group, values_from = c(n, pct_behind)) |>
  arrange(test, moment)
```

**Interpretation.** At every moment, pupils with lower mastery are more often
behind (band IV/V) than pupils with higher mastery: 64-83% versus 24-60%. The
difference does not disappear over time; at the end of Year 4, 83% of the lower
group is behind in maths, compared with 35% of the higher group. Note that the
end-of-Year-4 figures are based on only 29 pupils.

### 7g. The school's own maths tests

These are the tests that come with the maths method: after each block of
lessons, pupils take a test on what was just taught. They show whether pupils
keep up with the lessons, while Cito compares pupils nationally.

```{r rq2 math tests explore}
math_tests <- read_xlsx(here::here("data", "UvA_testresults_math.xlsx")) |>
  mutate(leerling = str_squish(leerling))

names(math_tests)
math_tests |> count(Cohort)
math_tests |> count(blok)
math_tests |> count(behaald)
math_tests |> count(toetsdoel) |> head(20)
range(math_tests$datum, na.rm = TRUE)
```

For each pupil we compute the share of test goals passed in Year 3 (blocks
3.x) and Year 4 (blocks 4.x). If the kindergarten goals prepare pupils for
Year 3, pupils with higher mastery should pass more Year 3 test goals.

```{r rq2 math tests per pupil}
# which year groups are in the file
math_tests |> count(year_group = str_sub(blok, 1, 1))

# % of test goals passed per pupil, Year 3
passed_y3 <- math_tests |>
  filter(str_starts(blok, "3")) |>
  group_by(leerling) |>
  summarise(n_tests_y3 = n(),
            pct_passed_y3 = mean(behaald) * 100)

# % of test goals passed per pupil, Year 4
passed_y4 <- math_tests |>
  filter(str_starts(blok, "4")) |>
  group_by(leerling) |>
  summarise(n_tests_y4 = n(),
            pct_passed_y4 = mean(behaald) * 100)

# add to the analysis dataset
rq2_data <- rq2_data |>
  left_join(passed_y3, by = c("pupil" = "leerling")) |>
  left_join(passed_y4, by = c("pupil" = "leerling"))

# how many pupils have test results, and how many tests each
rq2_data |>
  group_by(curr_year_group) |>
  summarise(n_with_y3 = sum(!is.na(pct_passed_y3)),
            mean_tests_y3 = mean(n_tests_y3, na.rm = TRUE),
            n_with_y4 = sum(!is.na(pct_passed_y4)))
```

```{r rq2 math tests analysis}
# lower vs higher mastery
rq2_data |>
  filter(!is.na(mastery_group)) |>
  group_by(mastery_group) |>
  summarise(pct_passed_y3 = mean(pct_passed_y3, na.rm = TRUE),
            pct_passed_y4 = mean(pct_passed_y4, na.rm = TRUE))

# regression
summary(lm(pct_passed_y3 ~ pct_mastered + age_year3 + factor(curr_year_group), data = rq2_data))
summary(lm(pct_passed_y4 ~ pct_mastered + age_year3 + factor(curr_year_group), data = rq2_data))
```

**Interpretation.** Pupils with higher mastery keep up better with the maths
lessons. In Year 3 they pass on average 85% of the test goals, compared with 67%
for pupils with lower mastery. In the regression, every 10 percentage points of
mastery goes with about 7 percentage points more test goals passed (b = 0.67,
p < .001, n = 58, R² = .46). The relation is still there in Year 4 (b = 0.89,
p = .001, n = 31), where pupils with higher mastery pass 70% versus 52%. In Year 3,
older pupils pass fewer test goals (b = -11.6 per year of age, p = .04); this may
be related to RQ1, as older pupils are often those who stayed longer in
kindergarten.

Two pupils in current group 4 already have Year 4 test results, although the
data ends before their Year 4; possibly they skipped a group or work at a higher
level in maths. Group 4 pupils also have slightly more Year 3 tests (35 vs 32),
probably retakes; this does not affect the percentage passed.

### 7h. Support in Year 3

Being on the waiting list also shows that the care team saw a need for extra
support. We therefore use two measures:

- **support need**: referred for academic support in Year 3 (started or on the
  waiting list);
- **support received**: academic support that actually started in Year 3.

A referral counts as academic if the support type is remedial teaching, a
language group or speech therapy, or if the need is learning, language or
speech & language.

```{r rq2 support need}
academic_needs <- c("Learning", "Language", "Speech & language")

support_need_y3 <- support |>
  filter(!is.na(student_name), !is.na(school_yr),
         started %in% c("Yes", "Waitlist")) |>
  filter(support_type %in% academic_types | need %in% academic_needs) |>
  inner_join(rq2_pupils |> select(pupil, curr_year_group),
             by = c("student_name" = "pupil")) |>
  mutate(group_at_time = curr_year_group - (2026 - (2000 + school_yr %/% 100))) |>
  filter(group_at_time == 3) |>
  distinct(student_name) |>
  mutate(academic_need_y3 = TRUE)

rq2_data <- rq2_data |>
  left_join(support_need_y3, by = c("pupil" = "student_name")) |>
  mutate(academic_need_y3 = replace_na(academic_need_y3, FALSE))

# how many pupils needed / received academic support in Year 3
rq2_data |> count(academic_need_y3, any_academic_support_y3)
```

```{r rq2 support analysis}
# share with support need / support received, by mastery group
rq2_data |>
  filter(!is.na(mastery_group)) |>
  group_by(mastery_group) |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            pct_need     = mean(academic_need_y3) * 100,
            pct_received = mean(any_academic_support_y3) * 100)

# average mastery of pupils with and without support need
rq2_data |>
  group_by(academic_need_y3) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_mastery = mean(pct_mastered, na.rm = TRUE))

t.test(pct_mastered ~ academic_need_y3, data = rq2_data)
```

**Interpretation.** 13 of the 60 pupils (22%) needed academic support in Year 3:
12 received it and 1 was on the waiting list. Pupils who needed support had
mastered on average 58% of the Year 3 goals at the end of kindergarten, compared
with 80% for pupils who did not need support, a difference of 21 percentage
points (95% CI 10-32, t = 4.12, p < .001). Lower mastery at the end of
kindergarten thus goes with a higher need for extra support in Year 3. With 13
pupils needing support, this result rests on a small group.

### 7i. Winter birthdays

Pupils born in October-December ("winter children") are a group the school
asked about specifically. We check (1) whether they master fewer Year 3 goals,
and (2) whether the relation between mastery and Year 3 maths is different for
them (interaction term `pct_mastered:winter_bdayTRUE`).

```{r rq2 winter}
# mastery and outcomes for winter vs other birthdays
rq2_data |>
  group_by(winter_bday) |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean_mastery  = mean(pct_mastered, na.rm = TRUE),
            mean_age_y3   = mean(age_year3),
            math_g3_mid   = mean(score_math_g3_mid, na.rm = TRUE),
            pct_passed_y3 = mean(pct_passed_y3, na.rm = TRUE),
            pct_need      = mean(academic_need_y3) * 100)

# does the relation with mastery differ for winter children?
summary(lm(score_math_g3_mid ~ pct_mastered * winter_bday + factor(curr_year_group),
           data = rq2_data))
```

**Interpretation.** 17 of the 60 pupils (28%) were born in October-December.
They were on average younger at the start of Year 3 (6.1 vs 6.3 years), so most
moved on to group 3 young. On average they mastered fewer Year 3 goals (68% vs
78%), scored lower on Cito maths in the middle of Year 3 (84 vs 109), passed
fewer maths test goals (71% vs 78%) and more often needed support (29% vs 19%).
However, once mastery is taken into account, a winter birthday is no longer
related to the maths score (b = -0.03, p = 1.00), and the relation between
mastery and maths is not different for winter children (interaction b = -0.22,
p = .64). In other words, winter children score lower mainly because they
mastered fewer goals; at the same level of mastery, they do as well as other
pupils. With 17 winter children these differences are descriptive and should be
interpreted with care.

## Limitations

- **Association, not effect.** Pupils who master more goals may simply be
  stronger learners; the data cannot separate the effect of teaching from the
  pupil's own ability.
- **Mastery, not teaching focus.** All pupils received the same kind of
  teaching; what varies is how much they mastered. Testing the teaching focus
  itself would require a comparison between groups that were taught
  differently (e.g. before and after the school introduced the focus, or
  between classes 1/2a and 1/2b).
- **Small sample** (about 60 pupils), from one school.
- **Linking by name.** Files are linked on pupil names; a spelling difference
  would cause a pupil to be missed.
- **Support records.** It is assumed that pupils without a record did not need
  or receive support. Only 13 pupils needed academic support, so this result
  rests on a small group.
- **Outcomes not available.** Repeating a year (only 1 pupil), well-being in
  Year 3 and the experiences of Year 3-4 teachers (no teacher questionnaire)
  could not be studied.
  
  
  ## Conclusion RQ2

**What we did.** For about 60 pupils (current groups 4-6) we measured how many of
the 15 goals the school set for the start of Year 3 each pupil had mastered at
the end of kindergarten, and related this to their results and support in
Years 3 and 4.

**What we found.**

- **Mastery varies a lot.** On average, pupils mastered two thirds (68%) of the
  goals, ranging from 13% to 100%.
- **Higher mastery goes with better maths and spelling.** Pupils who mastered
  more goals score higher on Cito maths and spelling in Year 3. For maths, this
  lead is still there at the end of Year 4. For reading speed (TMT) we found no
  relation.
- **They keep up better with the lessons.** In the school's own maths tests,
  pupils with higher mastery passed 85% of the Year 3 test goals, compared with
  67% for pupils with lower mastery.
- **They fall behind less often.** Of the pupils with lower mastery, 64-83% were
  in the bottom 40% nationally (band IV/V) at each moment, compared with 24-60%
  of the pupils with higher mastery.
- **They need less extra support.** Pupils who needed academic support in Year 3
  had mastered 58% of the goals, compared with 80% for the other pupils.
- **They start higher, but do not grow faster.** Maths progress from mid Year 3
  to end of Year 4 was similar for all pupils: the gap at the start of Year 3
  stays, but does not grow.
- **For winter children, mastery matters more than birth month.** Pupils born in
  October-December did worse on average, but this is explained by their lower
  mastery; at the same mastery level they do as well as other pupils.

**What this means for the school.** The 15 goals appear to be a meaningful
signal of readiness for Year 3: pupils who reach them start Year 3 at a higher
level, keep up better and need less support. Because the gap at the start of
Year 3 does not close by itself, monitoring these goals in kindergarten, and
giving extra attention to pupils who have not reached them, may be a useful
priority.

**How certain is this?** These are associations in a small group of pupils from
one school, not proven effects of the teaching focus. Pupils who master more
goals may also be stronger learners in general. To test the teaching focus
itself, the school could compare groups taught with and without this focus, for
example before and after the focus was introduced.
